name: Silicone chin implant

lead: A silicone chin implant is a shaped piece of soft silicone placed in front of the chin bone to add projection and define the profile. The change is visible straight away, once swelling settles.

It is among the most commonly used chin implant materials, and it can be removed easily. It is one of the standard hardmaxx chin options and is often compared with Medpor, ePTFE and bone-cutting sliding genioplasty. Published material consists mostly of case reports and surgeon series on complications and facial augmentation.

paras: The implant sits in a pocket over the chin bone and does not bond to tissue, so its position depends on how accurately the pocket is made. Choice of size and shape is made with the surgeon.
Reported issues include movement, buckling, bone resorption under the implant, infection (including late infection years after surgery) and soft-tissue deformity.

angle.text: A soft silicone implant is placed over the chin bone to add projection and sharpen the profile, and it can be removed easily. The change is visible straight away. Published material is mostly case reports and surgeon series on complications.

lead: A silicone chin implant is a solid, shaped alloplastic implant placed in front of the chin bone to increase projection. A general reference describes silicone as among the most commonly used chin implant materials: soft and flexible, but not bonding to tissue, so the pocket must be made precisely, with risks of movement, buckling or bone resorption; it can be removed easily [1].

In looksmaxxing it is classed as a hardmaxx option and is often compared with porous polyethylene (Medpor), ePTFE and bone-cutting sliding genioplasty [1]. Published material in the reviewed sources consists of case reports and surgeon series on complications and on facial augmentation.
infobox: Does not bond to tissue; removable [1]

paras: Silicone implants are available off the shelf and avoid a donor site, and artificial implants are described as biocompatible and FDA-cleared in general reference sources [1]. Because the material does not integrate with tissue, accurate pocket creation is stressed, and the implant can shift or buckle [1].

Alloplastic chin implants can be associated with infection, bone resorption and secondary soft tissue deformities, which typically appear early after surgery but may occur later [2]. A case report describes an infected silicone chin implant in a 67-year-old woman who had received it 25 years earlier, after nearby dental implant surgery with non-ideal positioning led to contact with the silicone implant and absence of osseointegration [3]. A separate paper describes revision of an infected alloplastic chin implant by immediate osseous genioplasty with wire fixation [2].

A 2025 single-surgeon series on facial feminization and masculinization surgery reports malar, chin and mandibular angle augmentation using fat grafting, stock silicone implants and custom implants [4].

The material reviewed contains case reports and a retrospective single-surgeon series rather than controlled trials: an infected-implant revision [2], an infected-implant case after dental implant surgery [3], and a retrospective review of facial augmentation in transgender patients [4]. No randomised comparison of silicone with other chin implants was found.
